analysis.one_liner: Imposes stiffer penalties and lets Labor seize goods from employers who run sweatshops.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to two House subcommittees in August 1989 and died there when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cracked down on garment-industry 'sweatshops' by raising the penalties employers face for paying below minimum wage, skipping overtime pay, or employing children unlawfully. It would have let the Labor Department seize garments from manufacturers who repeatedly violate wage and child labor rules, extended from two to three years the time workers have to sue for unpaid wages, and required federal wage, safety, immigration, and state enforcers to share information about suspected violators.
analysis.who_benefits: Garment workers — including homeworkers and many immigrants — who are underpaid or denied overtime would have a better chance of recovering what they are owed, with triple damages for repeat violations and an extra year to sue. Workers in other low-wage industries would also benefit from the longer statute of limitations on unpaid wage claims.

how_it_helps.text: Repeat violators of minimum wage, overtime, and child labor rules would owe triple back wages, face civil fines up to $10,000 per violation, and criminal penalties of at least six months in prison.

The Labor Secretary could seize garments, up to the value of the employer's liability, from garment manufacturers who violate wage or child labor rules more than twice in three years, and seize all garments made by homeworkers in violation of the law.
Workers would have three years instead of two to sue for unpaid minimum wages and overtime under federal wage laws.
Federal wage-and-hour and workplace-safety enforcers would have to share information on suspected violators with each other, with immigration enforcers, and with state labor departments.

analysis.who_pays: Garment manufacturers and other employers who violate wage, overtime, or child labor laws would pay higher damages, fines, and prison exposure, and could lose their goods to seizure. Compliant employers would face little direct cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers violating wage and child labor laws

drawbacks.text: Seizing a manufacturer's goods for wage violations raises due-process concerns; the bill answers with notice, a hearing, and return of goods once liability is paid, but a seizure power aimed at a company's inventory is a heavy enforcement tool.

Stronger penalties and a longer window for lawsuits would raise the cost of doing business in garment manufacturing, and critics argued such measures could push production offshore or underground rather than improve conditions.

The bill added new coordination duties across Labor, OSHA, immigration, and state agencies without any visible funding mechanism, raising questions about whether the referral systems would be staffed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers trapped in sub-minimum-wage conditions, the upside was substantial: real money recovered, real deterrence, and more time to sue. The costs fall almost entirely on law-breaking employers, though the seizure power is aggressive and enforcement coordination was unfunded. The main weakness was political, not design: with no cosponsors, the bill had no base of support to move it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, split between two subcommittees, and never came back out, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuck Schumer introduced the Sweatshops Prevention Act on August 3, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
Three weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Safety and the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where it sat with no further action.
The bill had no cosponsors, and no markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who violate minimum wage, overtime, and child labor laws avoided triple damages, bigger fines, and the possibility of having their goods seized. The garment industry's worst operators stayed exactly where they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers violating wage and child labor laws

for.name: Rep. Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sweatshops Prevention Act and advanced it to committee.

against.name: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee that controlled the bill's path to the floor
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees on August 24, 1989, and never brought it out for a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member besides Schumer signed on, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: Repeat violators of wage, overtime, and child labor rules would face triple damages, fines up to $10,000 per violation, prison exposure, and seizure of their goods. The bill's entire point was to make running a sweatshop cost more than following the law.
Employers using homeworkers outside the law's certificate system could have all garments they produced seized, targeting the hidden piecework economy where home workers are routinely underpaid.
